Question 1: I've worked on several hundred year old irreplacable old growth black walnut and I've worked on pallette furniture people have built. The wood species itself will have different properties, i.e. mahogany/pine...etc. Ultimately wood is wood and it behaves the same no matter what you paid for it or who gave it to you.

Question 2: I absolutely mean that. all the little bits you never see, leave it better than you found it. Give yourself something to be proud of and correct that other guy's mistakes.

Question 3: Long sleeves should do it, but those tyvek coveralls or jackets are what we use, they're very splash resistant. Thick gloves are a must, eye protection a must. You can get away with an N95 respirator, especially if you're outside. They're super cheap. Probably would eat through the tarp, if it doesn't, I'm pretty sure it will render it useless for future projects. I would just go on your lawn/driveway and hose it down when you're done, fuck the tarp.

Question 4: There is no one tool for your refinishing arsenal. Use all of the tools at your disposal. Paint scraper/Putty knives are great for big sections, razors are great for the corners and itty bits. She's probably trying to sell shit. If you think it will work, use it, if you're not sure, ask me.

You're welcome, don't be scared. You'll make mistakes, but thats a valuable part of the process. I would recommend however that you stain and cover with some sort of lacquer or shellac. Stripping painted wood is a super duper pain in the ass, that is if you ever want to change it in the future, which you might you never know. Stain and finish with wood grain visible always looks better. It would be great for me to see what we're talking about here too, sometimes the piece must be your guide and the wood tells you where it wants to go.
If when we strip the paint off we discover water stains under it (i.e. table was painted to hide them), does the stripper help with that too or is that another process to fix that?

This is one of those 'it depends on the wood' kinda deal. Pine is super porous, its capilary action will suck up just about anything, but its soft so its easily sanded, so water stains should be easily mitigated. Maple on the other hand has little grain and tends not to suck up too much, water included. Stripper would certainly get you going in the right direction, but 80 or 120 grit sandpaper should finish the job. Sometimes even this isn't enough, this is when I reach for the palm sander.

It also depends on the extent of the water damage, if its just spots, they should come out easily, if its rot...not so much.

I've also seen where water damage will eventually show through even paint, if this is the case it will certainly be harder to get out but not impossible. Last resort is 2 part wood bleach. This is not for the inexperienced.

I'm quite fond of the avant garde and the weirder the better. One wants what one wants and who am I to stifle that. Love your color idea, its bold and I like that, you have a vision so go with it. I can tell you this, spray paint is tough when you have to cover a LOT of surface. I mean, it will do the job but spray cans or rattle cans as I affectionately call them are thin. They have to formulate it thin so it can go through that itty bitty nozzle. Thin = Drips. I'm sure you see where I'm going. The secret here is slow and stead wins that race. Lots of very light and misty coats will ensure a drip free finish so don't ham fist it.

You're right about staining, I was staining table tops shabbily for about 6 months before I got really good at it. I'm going to post a video soon enough of how I do it as I just started /v/refinishing. Fixing that vernier is super easy, all you need is contact cement and a couple clamps. Let that contact cement dry on both surfaces first and get the line up just right because as soon as they touch, you won't be able to get them apart again. I prefer hide glue for this, but that shit is a stinky pain in the ass if you're not in a shop with a spanish guy that tends to the glue everyday.

Good job on stripping the drawer but you can see what I'm talking about if you don't actually use chemical stripper, shit takes for-ev-er. I could have each drawer done in 4 -6 minutes with the good stuff. Oh a side note on the paints, look at its chemical makeup, you can't really mix acrylics with lacquers and vice versa. I would use a poly if you want to throw a clear over it but watch how much you apply cuz shit can get yellow real quick and change the color of your base slightly.
